topic: Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning Disability
title: Safeguarding adults with a learning disability
blurb: Recognise abuse that targets people with a learning disability, apply the Care Act section 42 criteria and six principles, and act on closed cultures.
question: Liam, 27, has a mild learning disability and his own flat. His community nurse finds several new 'friends' staying there, his benefits gone within days of payment, and Liam saying he is scared to ask them to leave. What should the nurse do?

teach.h: When the local authority must make enquiries
teach.body: Under section 42 of the Care Act 2014, the local authority must make enquiries, or cause them to be made, when it has reasonable cause to suspect that an adult in its area has needs for care and support, is experiencing or at risk of abuse or neglect, and as a result of those needs is unable to protect themselves. In plain English: if a person who needs support may be harmed and cannot keep themselves safe because of their needs, the council must find out and act.

teach.h: Abuse that often targets people with a learning disability
head: Type
What it can look like
rows: Benefits taken, unexplained withdrawals, no food
Disclosure by sign or behaviour, injuries, fear of a person
People posing as friends to exploit
Home taken over by others, e.g. for drugs
Harassment or slurs because of disability
Rigid routines, shared clothing, no choice
Care needs, medicines or health left unmet
teach.caption: The statutory guidance lists types of abuse but says authorities should not limit their view of what abuse is.

teach.body: Liam, 27, has care and support needs, appears to be experiencing financial abuse and exploitation of his home, and says he is too scared to ask the visitors to leave. The nurse makes sure he is safe now, talks with him about what he wants to happen, explains that she needs to raise a safeguarding concern, and does so the same day. Because crimes such as theft may be involved, the police are informed. She records what she saw and what Liam said, in his words.

teach.caption: Abuse at Winterbourne View (2011) and Whorlton Hall (2019) came to light through BBC Panorama undercover filming.

items: Make sure the person is safe and listen calmly, using their communication (signs, symbols, objects).
Do not question repeatedly or lead; record what they said or signed, in their own words, with time and date.
Raise a safeguarding concern straight away under local procedures; tell the police if a crime may have happened.
Preserve any evidence and keep the person informed in a way they understand.
If they would have substantial difficulty taking part in an enquiry and have no appropriate person, an independent advocate is arranged (Care Act s68).

teach.h: Some acts are crimes whatever the person seems to want
teach.body: Sexual activity by a care worker with a person they support who has a mental disorder, including a learning disability, is an offence under the Sexual Offences Act 2003 (s38), and the person's apparent agreement does not change that. Ill-treatment or wilful neglect of a person who lacks capacity by a carer is an offence under section 44 of the Mental Capacity Act. Both must be reported as safeguarding concerns and to the police.

teach.text: Do not wait for proof or try to investigate yourself before raising a concern: the threshold is reasonable cause to suspect. And do not confuse empowerment with doing nothing: an adult with capacity leads on outcomes, but others at risk, or a crime, can still justify sharing information.

items: s42 criteria: care and support needs; abuse or neglect (or risk); unable to protect self as a result.
Six principles: empowerment, prevention, proportionality, protection, partnership, accountability.
Watch for financial and sexual abuse, mate crime, cuckooing and organisational abuse.
Closed cultures: families kept out, unrecorded restraint, mocking talk, fear of speaking up.
Care worker sexual activity (SOA s38) and wilful neglect (MCA s44) are crimes: report.

summary: You can now apply the section 42 criteria, use the six principles and Making Safeguarding Personal, and recognise abuse that targets people with a learning disability. You can also spot a closed culture and know which acts must go to the police.

A.q: A community learning disability nurse explains when a local authority must make safeguarding enquiries under section 42 of the Care Act 2014. Which set of criteria is correct?
options: Lacks capacity; at risk of harm; known to services
Care and support needs; abuse or neglect; unable to protect self
Aged 18 or over; eligible needs met; harm has occurred
On the GP register; lives independently; family concern
A.why: s42: reasonable cause to suspect the adult has needs for care and support, is experiencing or at risk of abuse or neglect, and as a result of those needs is unable to protect themselves.

whyNot.0: Lack of capacity is not one of the s42 criteria; many people with capacity are safeguarded.
whyNot.2: The needs need not be met by the council, and risk of abuse is enough without harm having occurred.
whyNot.3: These are not statutory criteria for a s42 enquiry.

A.q: A safeguarding lead says the team's response to a concern about Amira, 33, should be the least intrusive response appropriate to the risk. Which of the six safeguarding principles is this?
options: Protection
Prevention
Accountability
Proportionality
A.why: Proportionality means the least intrusive response appropriate to the risk presented.

whyNot.0: Protection is support and representation for those in greatest need.
whyNot.1: Prevention is acting before harm occurs.
whyNot.2: Accountability is about transparency in safeguarding practice.

A.q: On a visit to an assessment and treatment unit for people with learning disabilities, which finding is most suggestive of a closed culture?
options: Families discouraged from visiting and restraint not recorded
Patients choosing their own activities from a picture menu
Staff asking for a debrief after a difficult incident
An advocate visiting weekly and meeting patients privately
A.why: Keeping families away and leaving restrictive practice unrecorded are warning signs of a closed culture, where abuse can go unseen.

whyNot.1: Choice using accessible menus is a sign of a person-centred culture.
whyNot.2: Seeking debriefs is a sign of a reflective, open team.
whyNot.3: Regular independent advocacy is a protective feature.

B.q: Liam, 27, has a mild learning disability and his own flat. His nurse finds new 'friends' staying there, his benefits gone within days and Liam saying he is scared to ask them to leave. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Advise Liam to change his locks and to stop seeing them
Arrange a review of his support package next month
Raise a safeguarding concern today and inform the police
Ask his visitors to leave and then close the case
B.why: Liam meets the s42 criteria and crimes such as theft may be involved. The nurse should raise a concern promptly and involve the police, keeping Liam involved in decisions.

whyNot.0: This leaves Liam to protect himself when his needs mean he cannot.
whyNot.1: Waiting a month leaves him at ongoing risk.
whyNot.3: Confronting the visitors may increase risk, and the concern still needs to be raised.

B.q: Lucy, 22, has a learning disability and uses Makaton. During personal care she becomes very distressed, signs 'hurt' and points between her legs, and signs the name of a male visitor. What is the most appropriate first response?
options: Ask her detailed questions to establish what happened
Record what she signed, keep her safe and raise a concern now
Wait until her key worker returns to interpret her signs
Tell the visitor about the allegation to hear his account
B.why: Keep her safe, record her signs accurately in her own words without leading questions, and raise a safeguarding concern immediately; the police may need to be involved.

whyNot.0: Repeated or leading questioning can distress her and compromise any investigation.
whyNot.2: Delay leaves her at risk; staff can record what was signed now.
whyNot.3: Alerting the alleged abuser may put Lucy at risk and harm evidence.

B.q: Amy, 30, has a mild learning disability and capacity about her finances. She tells her nurse her brother takes most of her benefits each month, but she does not want 'trouble' for him. Nobody else appears to be at risk. What is the best approach?
options: Explore the outcomes she wants and the limits of confidentiality
Tell her brother that the nurse knows what he is doing
Close the matter, as she has capacity and has declined help
Apply to the court for a deputy to manage her money
B.why: Making Safeguarding Personal and the empowerment principle: work with Amy on what she wants, explain the limits of confidentiality, and keep offering support.

whyNot.1: Confronting her brother may increase risk to Amy and ignores what she wants.
whyNot.2: Capacity does not end the duty to offer support or to keep the risk under review.
whyNot.3: A deputy is for people who lack capacity; Amy has capacity about her finances.

C.q: A nurse learns that Dan, a support worker, has begun a sexual relationship with Jess, 28, a woman with a learning disability whom he supports at home. Jess says she is happy with it. What is the correct position?
options: It is a private matter as Jess says she consents
It is a conduct issue for his employer's HR process
It is acceptable if Jess has capacity to consent to sex
It is a likely care worker offence and a safeguarding concern
C.why: Sexual Offences Act 2003 s38: sexual touching by a person involved in the care of someone with a mental disorder, including a learning disability, is an offence; her apparent consent is not a defence. It must be raised as safeguarding and reported to the police.

whyNot.0: The care worker offence applies despite apparent consent.
whyNot.1: It is more than a conduct issue: it is a possible crime and a safeguarding concern.
whyNot.2: Her capacity does not remove the care worker offence.

C.q: Joe, 44, has a severe learning disability and is the subject of a section 42 enquiry. He would have substantial difficulty taking part and has no family or friend who could support him. What must the local authority arrange?
options: An independent advocate under the Care Act
An independent mental health advocate
A Court of Protection deputy for welfare
A relevant person's representative
C.why: Care Act s68: an independent advocate must be arranged for a safeguarding enquiry where the person would have substantial difficulty being involved and there is no appropriate person to support them.

whyNot.1: IMHAs support patients under the Mental Health Act.
whyNot.2: A deputy makes decisions for a person; it is not the advocacy the enquiry needs.
whyNot.3: A relevant person's representative is appointed under DoLS.

C.q: A night nurse finds that a care worker has repeatedly left Rosa, 60, who has a profound learning disability and lacks capacity, without fluids overnight 'because she makes a mess'. Which statement best describes the position?
options: It is poor practice best dealt with by supervision
It may be wilful neglect, a criminal offence to report
It is acceptable if fluids are given first thing next day
It is a matter for the care home's complaints procedure
C.why: MCA s44 makes ill-treatment or wilful neglect of a person who lacks capacity by a carer a criminal offence. It must be raised as safeguarding and reported to the police.

whyNot.0: Deliberately withholding fluids is more than a supervision matter.
whyNot.2: Withholding fluids overnight is neglect, whatever happens the next morning.
whyNot.3: A complaints process does not replace safeguarding and police reporting.

reteach.title: Needs, harm, cannot protect: then act
reteach.question: How do you decide quickly whether a situation needs a safeguarding concern?

blocks.body: Does the person have care and support needs? Are they being abused or neglected, or at risk of it? Do their needs mean they cannot protect themselves? If yes to all three, raise a concern. You need reasonable cause to suspect, not proof. Then work with the person on the outcome they want.

blocks.text: Apparent consent does not make a care worker's sexual relationship with a person they support lawful.

explain.body: Reasonable cause to suspect: care and support needs, abuse or neglect or the risk of it, and inability to protect self as a result. The duty applies whether or not the council meets the needs.

test.q: What level of certainty is needed before a local authority's section 42 duty is triggered?
options: Proof of abuse on the balance of probabilities
A police decision that a crime has occurred
Reasonable cause to suspect abuse or neglect
A written complaint from the adult or family
test.why: s42 is triggered where the local authority has reasonable cause to suspect the criteria are met.

whyNot.0: Proof is not required to start enquiries.
whyNot.1: A police decision is not needed; safeguarding and criminal processes can run together.
whyNot.3: Anyone can raise a concern; a written complaint is not required.

explain.body: Empowerment, Prevention, Proportionality, Protection, Partnership, Accountability. Making Safeguarding Personal asks the person what outcomes they want.

test.q: Which principle is about people being supported to make their own decisions and give informed consent in safeguarding?
options: Protection
Accountability
Partnership
Empowerment
test.why: Empowerment means person-led decisions and informed consent.

whyNot.0: Protection is support for those in greatest need.
whyNot.1: Accountability is transparency in safeguarding practice.
whyNot.2: Partnership is working with communities and services.

explain.h: Abuse that targets people with LD
explain.body: Financial abuse, sexual abuse, exploitation by people posing as friends, cuckooing (taking over a home) and organisational abuse are common risks. Look for changes in money, mood, visitors and routines.

test.q: Phil, 48, has a learning disability and staff help him manage his money. Which finding is most suggestive of financial abuse?
options: He spends most of his money on football tickets
Unexplained cash withdrawals and no money for food
He keeps his savings in a building society account
He has started buying presents for his new partner
test.why: Unexplained withdrawals and lacking basics despite receiving benefits suggest money is being taken.

whyNot.0: Spending on things he enjoys is his choice.
whyNot.2: Keeping savings in an account is not a warning sign.
whyNot.3: Buying presents can be a normal part of a relationship; it needs exploring only if other signs appear.

explain.body: Abuse at Winterbourne View (2011) and Whorlton Hall (2019) grew in closed cultures: isolated services, families kept away, unrecorded restraint, staff who mock patients and fear speaking up. Raise concerns early and escalate.

test.q: Kemi, a newly qualified nurse on an inpatient unit, sees staff mocking a patient and restraint left unrecorded. Her manager says 'that is how things work here'. What should she do next?
options: Escalate to senior managers and the safeguarding lead
Keep a private diary and wait for more evidence
Raise it at her next annual appraisal meeting
Speak to the staff involved and leave it there
test.why: Concerns must be raised promptly and escalated beyond a manager who dismisses them (NMC Code; raising concerns guidance); the safeguarding lead must be told.

whyNot.2: An appraisal is far too late for a safeguarding concern.
whyNot.3: Speaking to colleagues does not ensure patients are protected or the concern is recorded.
